summary: `ways[i][j]` = the number of paths from the start to (i, j). Since we can only move right or down, every path into a cell comes from the cell above or the cell to the left, so we add those two (T13 — DP on a grid).

blocks.title: Read the grid
blocks.text: `R C` on one line, then the program prints `Enter the grid:` and reads R rows as strings — we only need to look at each cell.

blocks.title: The DP table
blocks.text: One number per cell, all 0 to start. Build it with a comprehension so every row is its own list.

blocks.title: Fill row by row
blocks.text: Going top to bottom and left to right means the cell above and the cell to the left are always finished before we need them.

blocks.title: Blocked cell
blocks.text: No path can go through `#`, so it stays 0. This is checked first, so a blocked start or end correctly gives 0 paths.

blocks.title: The start
blocks.text: There is exactly one way to be at the start: stand still.

blocks.title: Add paths from above and from the left
blocks.text: The `if i > 0` / `if j > 0` guards matter: without them, `ways[-1][j]` on the top row would silently read the BOTTOM row.

blocks.title: Print the answer
blocks.text: The bottom-right cell holds the total. Answers can be huge, which Python ints handle.

pitfalls: No edge guards → `ways[-1]` wraps around to the last row.
